chapter: Chords, recordings and his own groups
title: Blue Harlem: the opening slow-blues solo
summary: He explains that Blue Harlem opened with his two-chorus guitar solo and sold the record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: 104 Q Savoy - 3 Riffs, 3 Barrons. - other record dates...
... Blue Harlem... This is another oddball thing. This particular tune, they wanted a guitar to start it off. And they named it Blue Harlem. So the guitar started it off with I think two choruses

And so I started it off -- real slow, funky home-town blues. A home -- with the red light outside -- slow blues -- where they turn the lights down way low. And I think we had to take a 2nd take. Cause I remember them releasing the talkin' and things like that, some other recording people like that up there -- a rehearsal. So, the second take was the one that came out & if my solo sold the record. And even Fred Robins used it for a theme song. He was a hell of a disc jockey at that time. He used it for a theme song and played only my solo, so, I made a mini-enemy, behind that think because I asked him at first, I say, man, the thing sell good, why don't you make a thing -- at that time the 45's were comin' -- I said put it on the juke box. That helps the musician out. But they didn't want to do it. Collector's item only. So, alright, the first chance I get I made it for somebody else I thought was gonna put it on the juke -- but it never ain't got on the juke box yet. I must have made that record 4 or 5 times ...
